it-2008-it-23.approach: Use the complement: "at least three share a birthday" fails exactly when either all $r$ birthdays are distinct or exactly one pair shares a day and everyone else is distinct. Subtract both from 1.

steps.title: Complement of the event
steps.body:
"At least three people share a birthday" is false exactly when no day is used by 3 or more people, i.e. every day is used by at most 2 people. Since the options only allow one shared pair, the complement is split as:

- $E_0$: all $r$ birthdays distinct;
- $E_1$: exactly one pair shares a birthday, all others distinct.

(Cases with two or more separate pairs are ignored by every option — the intended model is the textbook one below.)

steps.title: All distinct
steps.body:
Total outcomes $=365^r$. Ordered distinct choices: $365\cdot364\cdots(365-r+1)$, so
$$P(E_0)=\frac{365\cdot364\cdots(365-r+1)}{365^r}.$$

steps.title: Exactly one pair
steps.body:
Choose the pair: $\,{}^rC_2$. Give the pair a day: $365$ ways. The remaining $r-2$ people get distinct days different from that one: $364\cdot363\cdots(364-(r-2)+1)$ ways. So
$$P(E_1)={}^rC_2\cdot365\cdot\frac{364\cdot363\cdots(364-(r-2)+1)}{365^r}.$$

steps.title: Subtract
steps.body: $$P(\text{at least three})=1-P(E_0)-P(E_1),$$ which is option **(C)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: This is $1-P(\text{all distinct})$ = P(at least two share), not at least three.
This is $P(E_0)+P(E_1)$ — the probability of the complement, not of the event.
Removes both "all distinct" and "exactly one pair" from 1 — the required probability.
This is just $P(\text{all distinct})$.

pitfalls: Stopping at $1-P(\text{all distinct})$ — that answers "at least two".
Forgetting the factor $\,{}^rC_2$ for choosing which two people share.
